title: These Home Theater Projectors Give the Cinema Some Tough Competition
author: John Brandon
text: All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.I've seen some of the best movies and tested some of the best home projectors this year. Massively entertaining films like The Odyssey, Project Hail Mary, and Toy Story 5 have made 2026 a standout year for movies, and new home theater projectors like the Xgimi Titan Noir Max and the AWOL Vision Aetherion Max have upped the game in terms of beautiful, cinematic, color-accurate images at home.I've been reviewing the best TVs and projectors for years. That's why I put these latest home theater projectors to the test, running benchmarks to check for vividness, brightness, skin tone variations, and whether dark scenes look too washed out. I watched countless Netflix movies and 4K Blu-ray films—all for the cause. My main takeaway? These top models are giving the local cinema something to worry about. Bring some popcorn and a comfortable recliner, and you're basically there.For more TV recommendations based on our expert testing, check out our related guides, including the Best RGB TVs, Best TVs, Best Large TVs, Best OLED TVs, and Best Cheap TVs. The Xgimi Titan Noir Max won me over because of the dynamic, self-adjusting iris. As you watch a movie or show, the projector adjusts to allow more light in (for bright scenes) or closes to reduce light (for dark scenes). For example, during a nighttime sequence in the movie Hoppers on Disney+, the iris will close to make the blacks and grays look dark and richly detailed. That feature alone sets the Titan Noir Max apart.Most PopularGearWe Bought a $500 Counterfeit Luxury Watch. An early morning scene in the movie The Creator looked exactly like I would expect it to in real life, showing texture on the seaside cliffs. Even in a sun-drenched room, battle scenes in the movie War Machine looked bright and clear—outperforming the Hisense XR10 model.More functionally, it has four adjustable feet that allow you to adjust the height or even set the projector on a side table and angle it toward a wall.One downside is that, like many projectors, it doesn't natively run a streaming OS like Google TV, but I prefer to connect a Blu-ray player or Google TV Streamer anyway.SpecsRefresh rate240 HzWeight18 poundsHDMI ports3Light sourceTriple laserBest for GamingPhotograph: John BrandonPhotograph: John BrandonPhotograph: John BrandonPhotograph: John BrandonHisenseXR10 4K Smart Projector$6,000 $4,998 (17% off) Amazon$6,000 B&H PhotoI’ll never forget the first time I played the game 007 First Light projected on a wall in my house using the Hisense XR10. I felt very little lag using the low-latency mode, and the built-in speakers (the best I've tested on a projector) never felt lacking.The big and boxy XR10 is exactly what I would expect a high-end cinema projector to look like. It’s heavy at 23.4 pounds, but that’s because of its massive speaker and lens. Although I prefer the long adjustable legs on the Xgimi Titan Noir Max, the XR10 is stable and has a nicely subdued dark metallic look.The iris is adjustable (in seven different ways) to allow more light in or to make darker scenes even more vivid. Yet, of all the home cinema projectors I've tested in the last few months, the quick and easy setup on this model, plus a few unusual perks, made it a top pick.It's easy to configure, even though it uses the older Android TV operating system. I asked the onboard Google Assistant bot to start the install process and it only took a few minutes to do the whole thing. While the dark gray enclosure is understated, I liked how easy it was to adjust the focus and throw distance using analog levers on the top of the projector.At this price, the W4100i is not meant to compete with the titans of home cinema like the Hisense XR10, and it matches an older color gamut spec (Rec.709). The lumens rating is only 3,200, far below the Titan Noir Max's 7,000.Still, there are a few interesting perks with the BenQ W4100i. It has a mode that can match the 24p frame rate of movies for a more fluid look. With the refresh rate cranked to 240 Hz, playing the game NTE on my gaming laptop, I came to realize just how much I like using this projector for low-latency gaming. My controller flicks were rendered immediately during chaotic battle scenes.I’m not sure why BenQ insists on still using a dongle attachment for the operating system. You can skip it altogether if you use one of the HDMI ports for a Blu-ray player or another device. In the end, the lower-than-expected price, low latency, and easy setup are what sold me on this BenQ.Most PopularGearWe Bought a $500 Counterfeit Luxury Watch. The incredible 6000:1 contrast ratio and triple-laser light source are just the beginning. I’ve been impressed by the color accuracy, brightness, deep blacks, and extreme clarity across the entire image.Frequently Asked QuestionsWhy Use a Home Theater Projector?It’s an eternal debate—should you pull the shades, fire up a home theater projector, and watch a movie like you’re at the local cineplex? Or is it better to use a massive OLED or RGB television that will show a clearer image during a sunny day? Here’s my take after testing tons of the latest projectors and TVs: I prefer projectors for movies because I can max out the screen size to 120 inches or more. There’s just nothing like watching a 12-foot projected image of a movie with Dolby Atmos surround sound at home.What Do You Need to Use a Home Theater Projector?The short answer is quite simple: You just need a white wall. Purists will say a true home cinema experience requires a projector screen and a windowless room, and I have a testing room just for that purpose. However, all of the models I’m recommending are so bright and colorful that they perform quite well on a large wall without needing a projector screen. I do recommend room-darkening shades, though, because a darker room does create a better image.Why Are Home Theater Projectors So Expensive?Consumer-grade home theater projectors cost around $3,000 or more. In my experience, the latest large OLED and RGB televisions can easily cost just as much. I strongly recommend sticking to the $3,000 price point for a home cinema projector, though, because many midrange models (e.g., under $2,000) don’t look that colorful or bright.
